title: Why Is Everyone In Tech So Sad? | NOEMA
gist: An AI operations director argues that AI agents are not primarily an unemployment shock to knowledge work but a belief shock: by executing the work humans used to do, agents strip away the last justification for 'Workism' — the substitution of career for religion — and risk making an entire white-collar class stop believing in its own jobs. The load-bearing, non-obvious claim is that current layoffs are NOT actually driven by realized AI efficiency, and that the real corporate risk is a talent pool that declines to come back once companies try to rehire.

themes.theme: Angst Has Shifted From Economic To Existential

insights.claim: The current wave of white-collar disillusionment is qualitatively different from prior disruptions (recessions, outsourcing, earlier automation) because the questions workers are asking are existential rather than economic, which means conventional cyclical playbooks for labor-market recovery may not apply.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: If the driver is meaning rather than pay, wage increases and re-hiring campaigns will underperform as retention tools — watch for firms whose comp-led retention strategies fail to stem attrition.
insights.quote: What’s different about this moment is that the questions are not just economic but existential
insights.locator: We are, it’s true, living through a time of disruption

insights.claim: The cohort most insulated from economic upheaval — highly paid executives and senior professionals with decades of institutional knowledge, who should be best positioned to ride out AI's near-term impacts — are themselves uncertain about their career futures, indicating the doubt is not confined to junior or automatable roles.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Senior-leader disengagement is a leading indicator of execution risk at AI-transforming enterprises; watch unexplained executive departures, not just headcount cuts.
insights.quote: It strikes me as significant that the people who are usually the most insulated from economic upheaval, and seem to be well-positioned to ride out AI’s near-term impacts
insights.locator: It strikes me as significant that the people

insights.claim: Disillusionment about knowledge work spreads socially rather than individually — one person voicing it triggers agreement from peers — so the sentiment behaves like a contagion with sharp, nonlinear inflection rather than a gradual drift.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Morale collapse in knowledge-work organizations should be modeled as a step function, not a slow slide — engagement survey deterioration can go from benign to severe within a single cycle.
insights.quote: This disillusionment is infectious. One person speaks of it and others begin nodding: They too have felt it, the drop in motivation, the sense of being distant from their work, the lack of sleep, the concerns about the future.
insights.locator: This disillusionment is infectious

insights.claim: Observable early symptoms of the shift are consumption-side, not employment-side: knowledge workers taking up pottery, painting, crochet and other analog hobbies, and openly fantasizing about 'disappearing,' living on a farm, or going off the grid.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: The first tradeable expression of white-collar disenchantment may show up in craft/hobby and rural-lifestyle spend rather than in labor data — a demand tell that leads the employment tell.
insights.quote: Among my Knowledge Worker peers, I am hearing this more and more often: people who want to pick up pottery, painting, crochet or other old-timey analog hobbies.
insights.locator: Among my Knowledge Worker peers

insights.claim: 'Workism' — Derek Thompson's 2019 Atlantic framing of high-earning Americans seeking from careers the meaning, community and fulfillment that prior generations got from religion — is the mechanism that keeps talented people showing up to work that has little altruistic upside.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Treat white-collar productivity as partly faith-financed: a firm whose value proposition to staff is meaning rather than cash carries an unpriced liability if that meaning is disproven.
insights.quote: The best-educated and highest-earning Americans, who can have whatever they want, have chosen the office for the same reason that devout Christians attend church on Sundays
insights.locator: Workism: Praise Thee

insights.claim: Workism is explicitly framed as a psychological substitute product — manufactured to fill the hole a genuine vocation would otherwise occupy — which makes it a compensating good that fails precisely when the underlying work is exposed as unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Substitute goods lose demand instantly when the substitution is noticed; corporate 'mission' and 'purpose' programs are the most fragile part of the employee value proposition under AI.
insights.quote: That’s the true beauty of Workism: It is manufactured to distract people from the hole in their souls that a vocation would otherwise fill. It is the opiate of commuters in quarter zips.
insights.locator: That’s the true beauty of Workism

insights.claim: Because Workism depends on faith rather than logic, it has a specific structural failure mode: any paradigm shift that lets workers rationally interrogate the value of their output can break it all at once, unlike a gradual erosion of morale.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Look for a discrete break, not a gradient — the risk to human-capital-intensive firms is a regime change in belief, timed to visible AI capability jumps.
insights.quote: But Workism has a weakness. Like religion, it relies on faith’s triumph over logic.
insights.locator: But Workism has a weakness

insights.claim: Graduates are overwhelmingly channeled into finance, consulting and technology rather than vocations (teaching, nursing, firefighting, trades) that carry intrinsic social payoff, so the most credentialed labor cohort is concentrated in exactly the jobs most exposed to a meaning shock.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Elite-graduate pipelines into finance/consulting/tech are the highest-beta exposure to a Workism unwind — watch recruiting yields and acceptance rates at those employers.
insights.quote: Instead, graduates are overwhelmingly taking jobs in finance, consulting or technology.
insights.locator: But those aren’t the careers young people

insights.claim: David Graeber's 'Bullshit Jobs' taxonomy is invoked as an already-existing inventory of the specific white-collar behaviors AI makes indefensible: decks for projects that never launch, features nobody asked for, resting-and-vesting, and promotion-driven development where engineers optimize for what looks good at review time.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: The categories Graeber named are the exact cost lines executives will target first with agents — and the exact roles whose occupants already privately doubt their value.
insights.quote: promotion-driven development, where developers ignore what’s good in favor of what appears to be good when they’re up for a promotion
insights.locator: In “Bullshit Jobs,” David Graeber cataloged

insights.claim: Knowledge work's last remaining justification was that humans executed it — human thought, collaboration and creativity gave existentially meaningless output its life — and AI agents removing execution removes that final defense.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: The morale hit from agents is not proportional to jobs lost; it lands even where headcount is unchanged, so 'no layoffs' is not a hedge against the sentiment risk.
insights.quote: Knowledge work’s one saving grace, until recently, was that it was still executed by humans. We were needed.
insights.locator: Popping The Workism Bubble

insights.claim: The consensus vision among AI implementers — including the author, who runs AI operations at a creative technology company — is a future where all humans are managers of armies of AI agents, and he flags this as a view worth interrogating rather than accepting.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: A practitioner inside AI rollout publicly doubting the 'everyone becomes an agent manager' consensus is an early crack in the deployment narrative sold to boards.
insights.quote: It is common for people responsible for integrating these tools into their organizations, myself included, to describe the future of work as one in which all humans will essentially be managers of armies of AI agents.
insights.locator: Now, AI agents are increasingly executing

insights.claim: Agent usage in practice is escalating well past grunt work — employees under pressure to produce more are using agents to formulate complete business strategies, generate full marketing campaigns, build entire websites and draft strategy for whole divisions.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Agent scope creep into strategy and campaign work means services vendors in those categories face demand substitution sooner than the 'AI does the boring parts' narrative implies.
insights.quote: From a single email to an entire corporate strategy, the outputs of individuals, teams and organizations are increasingly generated in an instant by AI.
insights.locator: But in many cases, employees under pressure

insights.claim: Guy Debord's 'Society of the Spectacle' is repurposed as the operating model for modern work: Workism is a microcosm of the spectacle, a system in which appearing busy, important and knowledgeable is as valuable as being those things, and where work need only appear impactful.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: A useful lens for reading corporate AI announcements: much of the observable activity is signaling, and signaling budgets can be cut without the underlying business changing.
insights.quote: Workism is a microcosm of the larger spectacle: a world where appearing busy, important and uniquely knowledgeable is as valuable as actually being any of those things.
insights.locator: Debord’s Spectacle: I Don’t Wanna Do This Anymore

insights.claim: The core mechanism is that ~30 years of mediation (texting instead of talking, watching travel instead of traveling) has been incremental, and AI is the step that pushes abstraction far enough that the illusion becomes entirely visible to the people inside it.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Frames AI as a disclosure event rather than a productivity event — the risk is that it reveals how much existing output was never load-bearing.
insights.quote: with the introduction of AI, it is as if, over the past 30 years, we have been slowly taking steps away from the direct experience of life and work, and AI risks pushing us far enough that the illusion becomes entirely visible
insights.locator: And this is where things get particularly interesting

insights.claim: There is a direct conflict between what makes executives most excited about AI — less collaboration and fewer people — and the survival of the social structures that hold their organizations together, so the feature executives are buying is the same one that degrades the asset.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: AI-driven margin expansion may be self-limiting: the cost savings and the organizational decay come from the same lever, so early efficiency wins can precede later capability loss.
insights.quote: But what makes many executives most excited about AI — less collaboration, fewer people — risks dismantling the structures that hold the very organizations they lead together.
insights.locator: Organizations find themselves in a pickle

insights.claim: Firms will integrate AI regardless of the cultural cost because shareholders want it and near-term efficiency gains are too large to forgo, which makes the resulting organizational damage a near-certainty rather than a choice variable.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Don't underwrite management restraint — assume full AI deployment across white-collar firms and price the second-order human-capital consequences instead.
insights.quote: They want to integrate AI into their operations, as do their shareholders. And they will. In the short term, the potential efficiency gains are too good to pass up.
insights.locator: Organizations find themselves in a pickle

themes.theme: The Messy Middle As Hidden Productive Capital

insights.claim: Retention in knowledge work is driven by colleagues, bosses and the quality of the 'messy middle' experience — not by throughput — so gains in output speed do not convert into gains in talent retention.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Productivity-per-employee improvements from AI should not be assumed to reduce attrition costs; model retention and efficiency as independent, possibly opposing, lines.
insights.quote: Employees overwhelmingly choose to remain or leave their roles because of their colleagues and/or bosses, and the quality of the experience of the messy middle a workplace offers.
insights.locator: What’s At Stake: The Value Of The Messy Middle

insights.claim: Teresa Amabile's decades of Harvard Business School research on creativity (the Intrinsic Motivation Principle) holds that people do their most creative and innovative work when motivated by the work itself, and that political, risk-averse, relentlessly outcome-focused environments kill creativity — making 'messy' collaboration a precondition for valuable output rather than waste.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Gives an empirical basis for shorting the 'efficiency-maximized org' thesis: firms that strip exploration may see innovation output fall even as unit costs drop.
insights.quote: The environments that kill creativity are political, risk-averse and relentlessly outcome-focused. The environments that stimulate it are collaborative, idea-driven and free.
insights.locator: Research suggests this group needs that environment

insights.claim: The knowledge-work labor pool splits into two behaviorally distinct segments — 'outcome-first' workers who treat human needs and emotions as obstacles, and 'experience-first' workers who value collaboration, debate and shared struggle and often maintain artistic practices outside work.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: A segmentation for reading workforce risk: firms staffed with experience-first creative talent face far higher AI-transition attrition than outcome-first, metrics-driven organizations.
insights.quote: In my experience, there are two broad categories of Knowledge Workers. The first are outcome-first workers. Their focus is on the business, on winning, on efficiency.
insights.locator: But not everyone feels that way

insights.claim: Removing the messy middle has an explicitly asymmetric effect across the two worker segments — a victory for outcome-first workers, a foundational loss for experience-first workers — so identical AI policies produce opposite retention outcomes depending on workforce composition.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Diligence question for any AI-transformation story: which segment does this company's competitive advantage actually rest on?
insights.quote: For outcome-first people, it is a victory. For experience-first people, it undermines the foundation of work.
insights.locator: It’s important to note that the impact

insights.claim: The sports-officiating analogy (Hawk-Eye in tennis, the NBA challenge system, MLB's automated ball-strike system) is used to argue that technically correct outcomes can be subjectively worse for the product, because human error was part of what made the thing worth watching.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: A transferable heuristic: in experience-goods businesses, accuracy-maximizing automation can destroy the value it was bought to protect — relevant to media, entertainment and creative services.
insights.quote: Getting calls right 100% of the time may be objectively better, but it is subjectively less interesting and entertaining.
insights.locator: Klosterman argues that bad calls

insights.claim: The executive vision for AI-armed workforces converts work from an exploratory, learning-based process into assembly-line production — a transformation Debord anticipated in 1967 when he described intellectual professions being subjected to factory-like working conditions.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: If white-collar work industrializes, expect white-collar labor dynamics (turnover, deskilling, collective friction) to start resembling manufacturing rather than professional services.
insights.quote: In their vision for the future, work goes from a messy experience of learning and exploring to something more akin to assembly-line production.
insights.locator: Ironically, it’s a growing dream of executives

insights.claim: Inefficiency in knowledge work is defended as functional rather than merely tolerable — the messy middle is characterized as the condition under which genuinely valuable work gets produced, inverting the standard efficiency case for AI adoption.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: The strongest available counter-thesis to AI productivity narratives: efficiency gains may be measured on the wrong output variable entirely.
insights.quote: The messy middle, in other words, isn’t inefficient. It’s the condition under which genuinely valuable work gets produced.
insights.locator: Research suggests this group needs that environment

themes.theme: Layoffs Are Being Mislabeled As AI

insights.claim: An AI operations practitioner asserts flatly that the current corporate layoff wave is not actually caused by AI — AI automation is not yet creating anywhere near the efficiency gains needed to justify hundreds of thousands of job losses — meaning executives are attributing cuts to AI that have other causes.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Discount 'AI-driven efficiency' as an explanation in layoff disclosures; the cuts likely reflect demand or cost-cycle pressure, which means the promised margin durability may not be there.
insights.quote: Executives are often claiming these headcount reductions are a result of AI. They aren’t. At the moment, AI automation is not creating anywhere near the increased efficiency necessary to justify hundreds of thousands of lost jobs.
insights.locator: As I’m writing this essay, big companies are on a layoff bender

insights.claim: Layoffs are being announced at scale across big companies concurrently with the AI narrative, creating a credibility gap between stated AI efficiency and demonstrated AI efficiency that will eventually be tested against results.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Watch for the reconciliation: firms that cut on an AI story but cannot show the output gains will face either rehiring costs or visible capability degradation.
insights.quote: As I’m writing this essay, big companies are on a layoff bender. Thousands of people are being fired all over the place.
insights.locator: As I’m writing this essay

insights.claim: The central novel risk identified is that the historical hire/fire cycle assumed a fresh cohort waiting to be brought back, and this cycle may break — companies could go to replenish headcount and find that talent freed from Workism has moved on to different versions of their lives.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: The asymmetric risk in AI-era cost cutting is rehiring failure — model a scenario where the option to re-staff has a much higher strike price than history implies.
insights.quote: But what if talent stops coming back?
insights.locator: We’ve been through waves of hiring and firing

insights.claim: The switching costs that historically anchored knowledge workers to corporate careers have collapsed: the talent pool increasingly doesn't own homes and doesn't plan on having children, making a pivot away from corporate life easier than at any prior point.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Low household formation and non-ownership are usually read as macro weakness; here they are the mechanism that makes white-collar labor supply unusually flight-prone.
insights.quote: The talent pool increasingly doesn’t own homes and doesn’t plan on having kids, so it has perhaps never been easier to make a career pivot toward something that is genuinely satisfying in ways corporate life isn’t.
insights.locator: What if their side projects suddenly became profitable?

insights.claim: The workers most likely to exit are adversely selected from the employer's perspective — the most disillusioned, the most artistically talented or motivated, the most existentially sensitive, and the financially able — leaving behind those who stay by necessity rather than choice.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Attrition under this regime is quality-weighted, not random: expect measured headcount to hold while creative capability quietly degrades.
insights.quote: Some will certainly leave Knowledge Work — the most disillusioned, the most artistically talented or motivated, the most existentially sensitive to a sudden moment of enlightenment, the financially able.
insights.locator: Post-Workism: Escaping The Inescapable

insights.claim: The majority of knowledge workers will remain in place while the humanity of work erodes around them, producing a large population of retained-but-existentially-distraught employees rather than a clean labor exodus.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: The dominant scenario isn't mass quitting — it's mass disengagement inside firms, which shows up as declining output quality long before it shows up in turnover metrics.
insights.quote: But many more will remain, either by choice or necessity, to face a work experience where the humanity of work is eroding away.
insights.locator: Post-Workism: Escaping The Inescapable

insights.claim: A specific escape channel is flagged as newly viable — side projects becoming profitable — which converts what was previously a hobby into a competing income stream against corporate employment.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Platforms that monetize individual creative output are structurally positioned as the competing employer for exactly the talent enterprises most need to keep.
insights.quote: What if their side projects suddenly became profitable?
insights.locator: What if, when companies go to replenish headcounts

themes.theme: Dissatisfaction Gets Reabsorbed As A Commodity

insights.claim: Escape from corporate work is argued to be self-defeating in a specific, mechanical way: leaving to start a YouTube channel or Substack about abandoning your tech career turns the person and their life into a commodity that feeds the same system they left.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Predicts a durable supply of ex-tech creator content — content platforms benefit from the same white-collar disillusionment that damages the employers.
insights.quote: That’s the logic of the spectacle: It reabsorbs even the dissatisfied in order to sustain itself.
insights.locator: Post-Workism: Escaping The Inescapable

insights.claim: Founding a company is presented as an equally captured exit path, because a founder immediately needs to create a spectacle attractive to potential employees — meaning entrepreneurship reproduces rather than resolves the Workism problem.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Cuts against the assumption that disillusioned corporate talent flows productively into startup formation — the same meaning deficit follows them into the new company.
insights.quote: Or it might mean starting a company of your own, thereby suddenly needing to create a spectacle attractive to potential employees.
insights.locator: In today’s world, that might mean starting a YouTube channel

insights.claim: Debord's own biography is offered as the pessimistic base case for anyone betting on escape: he believed exit from the spectacle was impossible, dissolved his own movement rather than see it institutionalized, and drank himself to death in the countryside.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: A caution against romanticizing the 'off-grid' narrative as a real alternative economy — the author's own framework says it does not hold.
insights.quote: Debord believed escape from the spectacle was impossible. He went on to dissolve his own movement rather than watch it become institutionalized, and then drank himself to death in the countryside.
insights.locator: What would Debord say?

insights.claim: Debord's warning that dissatisfaction becomes a commodity once the economy of abundance can process it is applied directly to the present: anti-work sentiment is itself a monetizable product category rather than a threat to the system.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Treat the volume of anti-work and burnout content as a monetization signal, not a leading indicator of structural labor change.
insights.quote: dissatisfaction itself becomes a commodity as soon as the economy of abundance develops the capacity to process that particular raw material
insights.locator: Post-Workism: Escaping The Inescapable

insights.claim: The prescribed corporate countermeasure is deliberate under-automation: calling a colleague instead of querying an agent, doing work the old-fashioned meandering way accepting it will be slower, and ruling that certain work is reserved for human hands entirely.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: A concrete differentiator to watch for: firms that formally designate human-only work categories may retain creative talent competitors lose.
insights.quote: Or simply deciding that certain work is best left to human hands entirely.
insights.locator: Debord also believed the spectacle could be undermined

insights.claim: The most powerful recommended intervention is deflationary rather than motivational — reminding colleagues that the work is illusory and not important, on the argument that no one has ever died over a spreadsheet and almost no one will remember the work.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the standard corporate purpose-and-mission retention playbook; if this view spreads, employer branding built on world-changing claims loses potency.
insights.quote: No one has ever died over a spreadsheet. The world does not wait with bated breath for product launches. A marketing campaign will not change the world.
insights.locator: But perhaps the most powerful action of all

insights.claim: The author's constructive endpoint is a redirection of the meaning-seeking impulse from careers toward genuine local altruism and community impact, implying the demand for meaning does not disappear — it relocates outside the employer.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Meaning-seeking is a relocating demand, not a vanishing one — expect share of wallet and time to shift toward community, craft and volunteering at the expense of discretionary work hours.
insights.quote: perhaps we will be inspired to fill that hole with something real — true altruism, not its artificial Workism substitute — by actually trying to impact real people, in our communities, in real ways
insights.locator: And once freed from the false satisfaction

insights.claim: The framing question the essay leaves open is what happens to a society and its industries if an entire class of workers loses faith in their careers overnight — an explicitly untested, discontinuous scenario rather than a gradual trend forecast.
insights.speaker: Aaron Horwath
insights.so_what: Treat this as an unpriced tail scenario for human-capital-intensive sectors: no historical analog means no reliable base rate for recovery.
insights.quote: And what happens to a society and its industries if an entire class of workers loses faith in their careers overnight?
insights.locator: But this sweeping disenchantment begs a fascinating
